title: Process Supervision-Guided Policy Optimization for Code Generation

contributions.purpose: Overcome sparse, end-of-episode unit-test rewards in RL for code generation, which give no learning signal when code fails all tests, by producing dense line-level supervision.
contributions.mechanism: Automatically generate process-level supervision data by identifying the first error line in generated code via binary search, then train a Process Reward Model (PRM) on this data to emit dense line-wise signals during RL.
contributions.evaluation: PRM used to produce dense line-wise rewards during RL training of an in-house proprietary LLM; qualitative validation via visualized learned line-wise rewards (Figure 8) plus downstream pass-rate gains reported in C3.
contributions.source_quote: We propose an effective approach that automatically generates process-level supervision data by iden-tifying the first error line in generated code using binary search. We then train a PRM on this data to generate dense signals during RL training. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to demonstrate that PRMs can benefit RL from unit test feedback in code generation.

contributions.purpose: Determine how to properly integrate PRMs into RL training for code generation and distill a practical usage recipe.
contributions.mechanism: Systematic experiments comparing PRM integration strategies (DenseReward, ValueInit, and combined DenseReward & ValueInit) and PRM data selection strategies; key finding that using PRMs concurrently as both dense rewards and value-function initialization yields the largest improvement.
contributions.evaluation: Ablation on LiveCodeBench (LCB) and internal InHouseBench (IHB): combined DenseReward & ValueInit gives a relative increase of 5.7% on LiveCodeBench and 12.6% on InHouseBench over the RL baseline (Table 1); PRM data-selection comparison in Table 2.
contributions.source_quote: We conduct systematic experiments to determine how to properly and effectively integrate PRMs into RL. Our analysis explores various strategies for training a high-quality code PRM and utilizing PRMs to improve code generation. We summarize our findings into a practical recipe for successfully using PRMs in the context of code generation.

contributions.purpose: Demonstrate that the PRM-guided RL recipe improves code-generation pass rate, especially in long-horizon scenarios.
contributions.mechanism: Apply the recommended recipe (PRM as dense reward + value init) to RL training of the in-house LLM and analyze Pass@1 as a function of generated response length.
contributions.evaluation: Pass rate improved from 28.2% to 29.8% on LiveCodeBench and from 31.8% to 35.8% on the in-house benchmark; PRM gives ~9% overall Pass@1 gain and consistent improvement for responses longer than 100 tokens (Figure 3).
contributions.source_quote: By following the recipe, we significantly improve our in-house proprietary LLM's pass rate from 28.2% to 29.8% on the LiveCodeBench dataset and from 31.8% to 35.8% on our in-house benchmark. Besides, we find that integrating PRMs into RL training benefits code generation in long-horizon scenarios.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Building on these efforts, we sim-ilarly automate process supervision but differ in our primary objective. Rather than using PRMs solely as enhanced verifiers compared to Outcome Reward Models (ORMs), we focus on their integration into RL training for code generation.

While Wang et al. (2024a) provides preliminary results on PRMs improving RL training in the mathematical domain, their findings are limited. Our work offers a more thorough and systematic investigation of how PRMs can be leveraged in RL for code generation tasks.

notes: Absolute gains are modest (LiveCodeBench 28.2%->29.8%, ~1.6 points). Explicit trade-off/negative result: for responses shorter than 100 tokens PRM yields 'comparable or slightly inferior results' (PRM behaves like a biased ORM in short-horizon cases); benefit is concentrated in long-horizon (>100 token) responses. Main benchmark is a proprietary in-house LLM and in-house benchmark, limiting external reproducibility. Paper was rejected.
